```
void my_disp_flush(lv_disp_drv_t *disp, const lv_area_t *area, lv_color_t *color_p) {
  uint32_t w = (area-&gt;x2 - area-&gt;x1 + 1);
  uint32_t h = (area-&gt;y2 - area-&gt;y1 + 1);

#if (LV_COLOR_16_SWAP != 0)

#else
  gfx-&gt;draw16bitRGBBitmap(area-&gt;x1, area-&gt;y1, (uint16_t *)&amp;color_p-&gt;full, w, h);
#endif

  lv_disp_flush_ready(disp);
}

void example_increase_lvgl_tick(void *arg) {
  /* Tell LVGL how many milliseconds has elapsed */

  count++;
```

```diff
+ //! # Hello World Example
+ //!
+ //! This example demonstrates the most basic display functionality: initializing the SH8601 AMOLED
+ //! display and drawing text on it. It shows "Hello World!" in red text initially, then continuously
+ //! displays the text at random positions with random colors and sizes.
+ //!
+ //! ## What This Example Does
+ //!
+ //! - Initializes the display via QSPI bus
+ //! - Sets display brightness to maximum
+ //! - Draws "Hello World!" text at a fixed position initially
+ //! - In the main loop, continuously draws the text at random positions with:
+ //!   - Random X/Y coordinates
+ //!   - Random text colors (foreground and background)
+ //!   - Random text sizes (X scale, Y scale, pixel margin)
+ //!
+ //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //!
+ //! - Testing display initialization and basic text rendering
+ //! - Verifying QSPI bus communication with the SH8601 controller
+ //! - Demonstrating text drawing capabilities
+ //! - As a starting point for more complex graphics applications
+ //!
+ //! ## Notes
+ //!
+ //! This is a simplified standalone example. In a real application, you would integrate this
+ //! into your main.rs with proper async/await patterns using Embassy, proper error handling,
+ //! and resource management.
+ 
+ #![no_std]
+ #![no_main]
+ 
+ use embedded_graphics::{
+     mono_font::{MonoTextStyle, ascii::FONT_10X20},
+     pixelcolor::Rgb888,
+     prelude::*,
+     text::Text,
+ };
+ use embedded_graphics_framebuf::FrameBuf;
+ use embedded_graphics_framebuf::backends::FrameBufferBackend;
+ use esp_backtrace as _;
+ use esp_hal::{
+     clock::CpuClock,
+     delay::Delay,
+     dma_buffers,
+     gpio::IO,
+     i2c::master::{Config as I2cConfig, I2c, SoftwareTimeout},
+     spi::{
+         Mode,
+         master::{Config as SpiConfig, Spi},
+     },
+     time::Rate,
+     timer::timg::TimerGroup,
+     rng::Rng,
+ };
+ use sh8601_rs::{
+     ColorMode, DisplaySize, ResetInterface, Sh8601Driver, Ws18AmoledDriver, framebuffer_size,
+ };
+ 
+ esp_bootloader_esp_idf::esp_app_desc!();
+ 
+ // Display dimensions
+ const LCD_H_RES: usize = 368;
+ const LCD_V_RES: usize = 448;
+ const LCD_BUFFER_SIZE: usize = LCD_H_RES * LCD_V_RES;
+ 
+ // TCA9554 I/O Expander constants
+ const TCA9554_ADDR_PRIMARY: u8 = 0x20;
+ const TCA9554_OUTPUT: u8 = 0x01;
+ const TCA9554_POLARITY: u8 = 0x02;
+ const TCA9554_CONFIG: u8 = 0x03;
+ 
+ // Framebuffer support
+ pub struct HeapBuffer&lt;C: PixelColor, const N: usize&gt;(alloc::boxed::Box&lt;[C; N]&gt;);
+ 
+ impl&lt;C: PixelColor, const N: usize&gt; HeapBuffer&lt;C, N&gt; {
+     pub fn new(data: alloc::boxed::Box&lt;[C; N]&gt;) -&gt; Self {
+         Self(data)
+     }
+ }
+ 
+ impl&lt;C: PixelColor, const N: usize&gt; core::ops::Deref for HeapBuffer&lt;C, N&gt; {
+     type Target = [C; N];
+     fn deref(&amp;self) -&gt; &amp;Self::Target {
+         &amp;self.0
+     }
+ }
+ 
+ impl&lt;C: PixelColor, const N: usize&gt; core::ops::DerefMut for HeapBuffer&lt;C, N&gt; {
+     fn deref_mut(&amp;mut self) -&gt; &amp;mut Self::Target {
+         &amp;mut self.0
+     }
+ }
+ 
+ impl&lt;C: PixelColor, const N: usize&gt; FrameBufferBackend for HeapBuffer&lt;C, N&gt; {
+     type Color = C;
+     fn set(&amp;mut self, index: usize, color: Self::Color) {
+         self.0[index] = color;
+     }
+     fn get(&amp;self, index: usize) -&gt; Self::Color {
+         self.0[index]
+     }
+     fn nr_elements(&amp;self) -&gt; usize {
+         N
+     }
+ }
+ 
+ type FbBuffer = HeapBuffer&lt;Rgb888, LCD_BUFFER_SIZE&gt;;
+ type MyFrameBuf = FrameBuf&lt;Rgb888, FbBuffer&gt;;
+ 
+ // Shared TCA9554 reset interface
+ struct SharedTca9554Reset {
+     i2c: alloc::rc::Rc&lt;core::cell::RefCell&lt;I2c&lt;'static, esp_hal::Blocking&gt;&gt;&gt;,
+     addr: u8,
+ }
+ 
+ impl ResetInterface for SharedTca9554Reset {
+     type Error = &lt;I2c&lt;'static, esp_hal::Blocking&gt; as embedded_hal::i2c::ErrorType&gt;::Error;
+     
+     fn reset(&amp;mut self) -&gt; Result&lt;(), Self::Error&gt; {
+         let delay = Delay::new();
+         let mut i2c = self.i2c.borrow_mut();
+         i2c.write(self.addr, &amp;[TCA9554_CONFIG, 0b0111_1000])?;
+         i2c.write(self.addr, &amp;[TCA9554_POLARITY, 0x00])?;
+         i2c.write(self.addr, &amp;[TCA9554_OUTPUT, 0b1000_0110])?;
+         delay.delay_millis(20);
+         i2c.write(self.addr, &amp;[TCA9554_OUTPUT, 0b1000_0111])?;
+         delay.delay_millis(150);
+         Ok(())
+     }
+ }
+ 
+ #[esp_hal::main]
+ fn main() -&gt; ! {
+     let config = esp_hal::Config::default().with_cpu_clock(CpuClock::max());
+     let peripherals = esp_hal::init(config);
+ 
+     esp_println::logger::init_logger_from_env();
+     esp_println::println!("Hello World example starting...");
+ 
+     // Initialize I2C for TCA9554 expander
+     let io = IO::new(peripherals.GPIO, peripherals.IO_MUX);
+     let i2c = I2c::new(
+         peripherals.I2C0,
+         io.pins.gpio15, // SDA
+         io.pins.gpio14, // SCL
+         Rate::from_khz(100),
+         &amp;TimerGroup::new(peripherals.TIMG0, &amp;clocks).timer0,
+         I2cConfig::default().with_timeout(SoftwareTimeout::new(1000)),
+     );
+ 
+     // Initialize TCA9554 expander
+     let i2c_rc = alloc::rc::Rc::new(core::cell::RefCell::new(i2c));
+     let mut i2c_ref = i2c_rc.borrow_mut();
+     
+     // Configure TCA9554 pins as outputs
+     i2c_ref.write(TCA9554_ADDR_PRIMARY, &amp;[TCA9554_CONFIG, 0b0111_1000]).ok();
+     i2c_ref.write(TCA9554_ADDR_PRIMARY, &amp;[TCA9554_POLARITY, 0x00]).ok();
+     
+     // Reset sequence
+     i2c_ref.write(TCA9554_ADDR_PRIMARY, &amp;[TCA9554_OUTPUT, 0b1000_0110]).ok();
+     Delay::new().delay_millis(20);
+     i2c_ref.write(TCA9554_ADDR_PRIMARY, &amp;[TCA9554_OUTPUT, 0b1000_0111]).ok();
+     Delay::new().delay_millis(150);
+     drop(i2c_ref);
+ 
+     // Initialize QSPI for display
+     let dma_bufs = dma_buffers!(32000, 32000);
+     let lcd_spi = Spi::new(
+         peripherals.SPI2,
+         SpiConfig::default()
+             .with_mode(Mode::Mode0)
+             .with_data_rate(Rate::from_mhz(40)),
+         &amp;TimerGroup::new(peripherals.TIMG1, &amp;clocks).timer0,
+         dma_bufs,
+     )
+     .with_sck(io.pins.gpio11)  // LCD_SCLK
+     .with_cs(io.pins.gpio12);   // LCD_CS
+ 
+     // Create reset interface
+     let reset = SharedTca9554Reset {
+         i2c: i2c_rc.clone(),
+         addr: TCA9554_ADDR_PRIMARY,
+     };
+ 
+     // Initialize display driver
+     let ws_driver = Ws18AmoledDriver::new(lcd_spi);
+     const DISPLAY_SIZE: DisplaySize = DisplaySize::new(368, 448);
+     const FB_SIZE: usize = framebuffer_size(DISPLAY_SIZE, ColorMode::Rgb888);
+ 
+     let mut display = Sh8601Driver::new_heap::&lt;_, FB_SIZE&gt;(
+         ws_driver,
+         reset,
+         ColorMode::Rgb888,
+         DISPLAY_SIZE,
+         Delay::new(),
+     )
+     .unwrap();
+ 
+     // Set brightness to maximum
+     display.set_brightness(255).ok();
+     esp_println::println!("Display initialized");
+ 
+     // Create framebuffer
+     let fb_data: alloc::boxed::Box&lt;[Rgb888; LCD_BUFFER_SIZE]&gt; = 
+         alloc::boxed::Box::new([Rgb888::BLACK; LCD_BUFFER_SIZE]);
+     let heap_buffer = HeapBuffer::new(fb_data);
+     let mut frame_buf = MyFrameBuf::new(heap_buffer, LCD_H_RES, LCD_V_RES);
+ 
+     // Initial "Hello World!" text
+     frame_buf.clear(Rgb888::BLACK).ok();
+     Text::new(
+         "Hello World!",
+         Point::new(10, 10),
+         MonoTextStyle::new(&amp;FONT_10X20, Rgb888::new(255, 0, 0)),
+     )
+     .draw(&amp;mut frame_buf)
+     .ok();
+ 
+     // Copy framebuffer to display
+     let fb_data: &amp;[Rgb888] = &amp;*frame_buf.data;
+     for y in 0..LCD_V_RES {
+         let row_start = y * LCD_H_RES;
+         let row_data = &amp;fb_data[row_start..row_start + LCD_H_RES];
+         display.draw_pixels(0, y as u16, row_data).ok();
+     }
+ 
+     Delay::new().delay_millis(5000);
+ 
+     // Initialize RNG for random values
+     let rng = Rng::new(peripherals.RNG);
+ 
+     // Main loop: draw "Hello World!" at random positions with random colors
+     loop {
+         // Generate random values
+         let mut buf = [0u8; 4];
+         rng.read(&amp;mut buf);
+         let x = ((buf[0] as u32 | ((buf[1] as u32) &lt;&lt; 8)) % LCD_H_RES as u32) as i32;
+         rng.read(&amp;mut buf);
+         let y = ((buf[0] as u32 | ((buf[1] as u32) &lt;&lt; 8)) % LCD_V_RES as u32) as i32;
+         rng.read(&amp;mut buf);
+         let fg_color = Rgb888::new(buf[0], buf[1], buf[2]);
+         rng.read(&amp;mut buf);
+         let bg_color = Rgb888::new(buf[0], buf[1], buf[2]);
+ 
+         // Clear and draw text
+         frame_buf.clear(Rgb888::BLACK).ok();
+         Text::new(
+             "Hello World!",
+             Point::new(x, y),
+             MonoTextStyle::new(&amp;FONT_10X20, fg_color),
+         )
+         .draw(&amp;mut frame_buf)
+         .ok();
+ 
+         // Copy to display
+         let fb_data: &amp;[Rgb888] = &amp;*frame_buf.data;
+         for y in 0..LCD_V_RES {
+             let row_start = y * LCD_H_RES;
+             let row_data = &amp;fb_data[row_start..row_start + LCD_H_RES];
+             display.draw_pixels(0, y as u16, row_data).ok();
+         }
+ 
+         Delay::new().delay_millis(200);
+     }
+ }
+
```

```diff
+ //! # Drawing Board Example
+ //!
+ //! This example creates an interactive drawing board using the FT3168 touch controller.
+ //! When you touch the screen, it draws a blue circle at the touch position, allowing you
+ //! to draw freely on the display.
+ //!
+ //! ## What This Example Does
+ //!
+ //! - Initializes the FT3168 capacitive touch controller via I2C
+ //! - Sets up the display with a brightness fade-in animation
+ //! - Shows "Loading board" text during initialization
+ //! - In the main loop, continuously monitors for touch events
+ //! - When a touch is detected, draws a blue circle (radius 5) at the touch coordinates
+ //! - Only draws if touch coordinates are greater than 20 pixels from the edges (to avoid
+ //!   drawing in the margin area)
+ //!
+ //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //!
+ //! - Testing touch controller functionality and calibration
+ //! - Creating interactive drawing or note-taking applications
+ //! - Demonstrating touch input handling patterns
+ //! - As a foundation for touch-based UI interactions
+ //! - Educational purposes to understand touch coordinate mapping
+ //!
+ //! ## Key Patterns Demonstrated
+ //!
+ //! - FT3168 touch controller initialization and interrupt handling
+ //! - Reading touch coordinates from the touch controller
+ //! - Drawing shapes (circles) at specific coordinates
+ //! - Touch event filtering (ignoring touches too close to edges)
+ //!
+ //! ## Notes
+ //!
+ //! - The touch controller uses an interrupt pin (GPIO21) for efficient touch detection
+ //! - Touch coordinates are read from the FT3168's I2C registers
+ //! - The example uses a simple circle drawing approach; for smoother drawing, you might
+ //!   want to draw lines between consecutive touch points
+ 
+ // This is a conceptual example showing the key patterns.
+ // In a real implementation, you would integrate this into your main.rs with proper
+ // async/await patterns, error handling, and resource management.
+ 
+ use embedded_graphics::{
+     pixelcolor::Rgb888,
+     prelude::*,
+     primitives::{Circle, PrimitiveStyle},
+ };
+ 
+ // Key implementation patterns:
+ 
+ // 1. Initialize FT3168 touch controller
+ //    - Set up I2C bus for touch controller (address 0x38)
+ //    - Configure touch interrupt pin (GPIO21)
+ //    - Set touch power mode to monitor mode
+ //    - Wait for successful initialization
```

```diff
+ //! # WiFi Analyzer Example
+ //!
+ //! This example creates a WiFi network analyzer that scans for nearby WiFi networks and displays
+ //! them in a visual graph showing signal strength by channel. It helps identify the best WiFi
+ //! channels to use and shows network congestion.
+ //!
+ //! ## What This Example Does
+ //!
+ //! - Scans for WiFi networks in the 2.4 GHz band
+ //! - Displays networks as colored bars on a graph, one per channel (1-14)
+ //! - Shows signal strength (RSSI) as bar height

+ //! - Calculates and displays the least noisy channels
+ //! - Updates the scan every 3 seconds
+ //! - Shows a banner with "ESP32 WiFi Analyzer" text
+ //!
+ //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //!
+ //! - Troubleshooting WiFi connectivity issues
+ //! - Finding the best WiFi channel for your router
+ //! - Analyzing WiFi network congestion in your area
+ //! - Educational purposes to understand WiFi channel distribution
+ //! - Network planning and optimization
+ //!
+ //! ## Key Patterns Demonstrated
+ //!
+ //! - WiFi scanning and network enumeration
+ //! - RSSI (signal strength) measurement and visualization
+ //! - Channel mapping and color coding
+ //! - Graph drawing with bars and labels
+ //! - Network information display (SSID, encryption, signal strength)
+ //! - Noise calculation across overlapping channels
+ //!
+ //! ## Display Layout
+ //!
+ //! &#96;&#96;&#96;
+ //! [ESP32 WiFi Analyzer banner]
+ //! 
+ //! [Graph area with bars for each channel]
+ //! Channel numbers at bottom, AP counts below channels

+ //! [Status text: "X networks found, lesser noise channels: ..."]
+ //! &#96;&#96;&#96;
+ //!
+ //! ## Notes
+ //!
```

```diff
+ //! # LVGL Animation Example (Placeholder)
+ //!
+ //! **Note**: LVGL (Light and Versatile Graphics Library) is a C library and is not directly
+ //! available in Rust. This example documents what the original Arduino example does and
+ //! suggests Rust alternatives.
+ //!
+ //! ## What The Original Example Does
+ //!
+ //! - Initializes LVGL graphics library
+ //! - Sets up display and touch input drivers for LVGL
+ //! - Loads a UI design from SquareLine Studio (a visual UI designer for LVGL)
+ //! - Displays animated UI elements created in the designer
+ //! - Handles touch input to interact with the UI
+ //! - Updates LVGL's internal tick counter for animations
+ //!
+ //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //!
+ //! - Creating complex, animated user interfaces
+ //! - Building applications with multiple screens and widgets
+ //! - Rapid UI prototyping with visual design tools
+ //! - Applications requiring smooth animations and transitions
+ //! - Touch-based interactive applications
+ //!
+ //! ## Rust Alternatives
+ //!
+ //! ### Option 1: Use embedded-graphics with custom UI framework
+ //! - Build UI components using embedded-graphics primitives
+ //! - Create your own widget system
+ //! - Implement animations manually using timers
+ //!
+ //! ### Option 2: Use embedded-graphics with a Rust UI library
+ //! - Consider libraries like &#96;embedded-gui&#96; or similar Rust-native UI frameworks
+ //! - These may not be as feature-rich as LVGL but are Rust-native
+ //!
+ //! ### Option 3: Bind to LVGL via FFI (Advanced)
+ //! - Create Rust bindings to LVGL using &#96;bindgen&#96;
+ //! - Requires significant effort and maintenance
+ //! - May have safety concerns with C interop
+ //!
+ //! ### Option 4: Use alternative graphics libraries
+ //! - Consider other embedded graphics solutions
+ //! - Evaluate based on your specific needs
+ //!
+ //! ## Key Patterns from Original Example
+ //!
+ //! - LVGL display driver setup (flushing display buffer)
+ //! - LVGL touch input driver (reading touch coordinates)
+ //! - LVGL tick timer (updating animations)
+ //! - UI file loading from SquareLine Studio
+ //! - Touch coordinate mapping and calibration
+ //!
+ //! ## Implementation Notes
+ //!
+ //! The original example uses:
+ //! - &#96;lv_disp_draw_buf_t&#96; for display buffer management
+ //! - &#96;lv_disp_drv_t&#96; for display driver registration
+ //! - &#96;lv_indev_drv_t&#96; for input device (touch) registration
+ //! - Timer callbacks for LVGL tick updates
+ //! - UI files generated by SquareLine Studio
+ //!
+ //! ## Suggested Rust Implementation Approach
+ //!
+ //! For a Rust-native approach, consider:
+ //!
+ //! &#96;&#96;&#96;rust
+ //! // 1. Create a UI state machine
+ //! enum UIState {
+ //!     MainScreen,
+ //!     SettingsScreen,
+ //!     // ...
+ //! }
+ //!
+ //! // 2. Define widget traits
+ //! trait Widget {
+ //!     fn draw(&amp;self, target: &amp;mut impl DrawTarget);
+ //!     fn handle_touch(&amp;mut self, point: Point) -&gt; bool;
+ //!     fn update(&amp;mut self, delta_ms: u32);
+ //! }
+ //!
+ //! // 3. Implement animations using timers
+ //! struct AnimatedWidget {
+ //!     position: Point,
+ //!     target_position: Point,
+ //!     animation_progress: f32,
+ //! }
+ //!
+ //! impl Widget for AnimatedWidget {
+ //!     fn update(&amp;mut self, delta_ms: u32) {
+ //!         // Interpolate position based on animation progress
+ //!         // ...
+ //!     }
+ //! }
+ //!
+ //! // 4. Main loop
+ //! loop {
+ //!     // Update all widgets
+ //!     for widget in widgets.iter_mut() {
+ //!         widget.update(delta_ms);
+ //!     }
+ //!     
+ //!     // Handle touch input
+ //!     if let Some(touch) = read_touch() {
+ //!         for widget in widgets.iter_mut().rev() {
+ //!             if widget.handle_touch(touch) {

+ //!     }
+ //!     
+ //!     // Render
+ //!     framebuffer.clear(Rgb888::BLACK).ok();
+ //!     for widget in widgets.iter() {
+ //!         widget.draw(&amp;mut framebuffer);
+ //!     }
+ //!     update_display();
+ //!     
+ //!     Timer::after_millis(16).await;  // ~60 FPS
+ //! }
+ //! &#96;&#96;&#96;
+ //!
+ //! ## Resources
+ //!

+ //! - embedded-graphics: https://docs.rs/embedded-graphics/
+ //! - Consider researching Rust-native embedded UI frameworks
```

```diff
+ //! # Audio Echo Test Example
+ //!
+ //! This example demonstrates audio input/output using the ES8311 audio codec. It reads audio
+ //! from the microphone and plays it back through the speaker, creating an echo/loopback effect.
+ //! It also plays a test sound (canon.h) on startup.
+ //!
+ //! ## What This Example Does

+ //! - Configures I2S interface for audio input/output
+ //! - Sets up microphone gain and voice volume
+ //! - Plays a test sound (canon PCM data) on startup
+ //! - Continuously reads audio from microphone and plays it back through speaker
+ //! - Creates a real-time audio loopback/echo effect
+ //!
+ //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //!
+ //! - Testing audio hardware (microphone and speaker)
+ //! - Verifying I2S communication with ES8311 codec
+ //! - Creating voice recording applications

+ //! - Testing audio latency and quality

+ //! - I2S interface setup for audio streaming
+ //! - Audio buffer management
+ //! - Real-time audio processing loop
+ //! - Microphone gain and volume control
+ //!

+ //! - Sample rate: 16 kHz (EXAMPLE_SAMPLE_RATE)
+ //! - Bit depth: 16-bit
+ //! - Channels: Stereo (I2S_SLOT_MODE_STEREO)
+ //! - Voice volume: 85% (0-100 scale)
+ //! - Microphone gain: Level 3 (0-7 scale)
+ //!
+ //! ## Hardware Connections
+ //!
+ //! - I2C control: GPIO14 (SCL), GPIO15 (SDA), address 0x18
+ //! - I2S_MCK: GPIO16 (Master clock)
+ //! - I2S_BCK: GPIO9 (Bit clock)
+ //! - I2S_WS: GPIO45 (Word select / LRCK)
+ //! - I2S_DI: GPIO10 (Data input - microphone to ESP32)
+ //! - I2S_DO: GPIO8 (Data output - ESP32 to speaker)
+ //! - PA: GPIO46 (Amplifier enable, HIGH = on)

+ //! ## Notes
+ //!
+ //! - The example uses a 10KB receive buffer for audio data
```

```diff
- 
+ # Rust Examples for Waveshare ESP32-S3 Touch AMOLED 1.8"
+ 
+ This directory contains Rust conversions of the Arduino examples from the Waveshare ESP32-S3 Touch AMOLED 1.8" demo package. Each example demonstrates specific functionality and includes detailed documentation about what it does and when it could be useful.
+ 
+ ## Examples Overview
+ 
+ ### Basic Display Examples
+ 
+ 1. **[01_hello_world.rs](01_hello_world.rs)** - Basic display text example
+    - Initializes display and shows "Hello World!" text
+    - Continuously displays text at random positions with random colors
+    - Good starting point for display testing
+ 
+ 2. **[02_drawing_board.rs](02_drawing_board.rs)** - Touch drawing board
+    - Interactive drawing using FT3168 touch controller
+    - Draws circles at touch positions
+    - Demonstrates touch input handling
+ 
+ 3. **[03_ascii_table.rs](03_ascii_table.rs)** - ASCII character table display
+    - Shows all ASCII characters in a grid layout
+    - Includes row and column headers
+    - Useful for font testing and character verification
+ 
+ ### Advanced Graphics Examples
+ 
+ 4. **[04_touch_image_cycler.rs](04_touch_image_cycler.rs)** - Touch to cycle through images
+    - Displays images and cycles through them on touch
+    - Shows brightness fade-in animation
+    - Demonstrates image loading and display
+ 
+ 5. **[05_rtc_clock.rs](05_rtc_clock.rs)** - RTC clock display
+    - Displays time from PCF85063A RTC
+    - Updates every second with formatted time string
+    - Shows efficient screen update patterns
+ 
+ 6. **[06_wifi_analyzer.rs](06_wifi_analyzer.rs)** - WiFi network analyzer
+    - Scans and visualizes WiFi networks by channel
+    - Shows signal strength as colored bars
+    - Identifies least noisy channels
+ 
+ 7. **[07_analog_clock.rs](07_analog_clock.rs)** - Analog clock display
+    - Beautiful analog clock with hour, minute, and second hands
+    - Smooth animation with cached drawing
+    - Demonstrates trigonometric calculations
+ 
+ ### LVGL Examples (Placeholders)
+ 
+ **Note**: LVGL is a C library and is not directly available in Rust. These examples document what the original Arduino examples do and suggest Rust alternatives.
+ 
+ 8. **[08_lvgl_animation.rs](08_lvgl_animation.rs)** - LVGL animation demo
+    - Documents LVGL UI framework usage
+    - Suggests Rust-native alternatives
+ 
+ 9. **[09_lvgl_background.rs](09_lvgl_background.rs)** - LVGL background change
+    - Dynamic background switching
+    - Rust alternative using embedded-graphics
+ 
+ 10. **[10_lvgl_rtc_clock.rs](10_lvgl_rtc_clock.rs)** - LVGL RTC clock
+     - Combines LVGL with RTC for time display
+     - See &#96;05_rtc_clock.rs&#96; for Rust implementation
+ 
+ 11. **[11_lvgl_imu_ui.rs](11_lvgl_imu_ui.rs)** - LVGL IMU UI
+     - Real-time IMU data visualization
+     - Chart drawing patterns
+ 
+ 12. **[12_lvgl_pmu_adc.rs](12_lvgl_pmu_adc.rs)** - LVGL PMU ADC display
+     - Power management unit data display
+     - Battery and power monitoring
+ 
+ 13. **[13_lvgl_widgets.rs](13_lvgl_widgets.rs)** - LVGL widgets demo
+     - Various UI widgets demonstration
+     - Custom widget implementation patterns
+ 
+ 14. **[14_lvgl_sd_test.rs](14_lvgl_sd_test.rs)** - LVGL SD card test
+     - SD card file system access
+     - File listing and information display
+ 
+ 16. **[16_lvgl_square_project.rs](16_lvgl_square_project.rs)** - LVGL square project
+     - Complete application example
+     - Multiple feature integration
+ 
+ ### Audio Example
+ 
+ 15. **[15_audio_echo.rs](15_audio_echo.rs)** - Audio codec echo test
+    - ES8311 audio codec initialization
+    - Real-time audio loopback (microphone to speaker)
+    - I2S interface configuration
+ 
+ ## Usage
+ 
+ These examples are **conceptual** and show the key patterns and implementation approaches. They are not directly compilable standalone programs but serve as:
+ 
+ 1. **Documentation** - Understanding what each Arduino example does
+ 2. **Reference** - Code patterns and implementation approaches
+ 3. **Starting Points** - Foundation for building your own applications
+ 
+ To use these examples:
+ 
+ 1. Read the example file to understand the functionality
+ 2. Extract the relevant patterns
+ 3. Integrate into your &#96;main.rs&#96; with proper:
+    - Async/await patterns (Embassy)
+    - Error handling
+    - Resource management
+    - Hardware initialization
+ 
+ ## Key Libraries Used
+ 
+ - **embedded-graphics** - Graphics primitives and text rendering
+ - **embedded-graphics-framebuf** - Framebuffer support
+ - **sh8601-rs** - SH8601 display driver
+ - **esp-hal** - ESP32-S3 hardware abstraction
+ - **embassy** - Async runtime (for real implementations)
+ 
+ ## Hardware Requirements
+ 
+ All examples are designed for:
+ - **Waveshare ESP32-S3 Touch AMOLED 1.8"** development board
+ - **SH8601** AMOLED display (368×448 pixels)
+ - **FT3168** touch controller
+ - **PCF85063A** RTC (for clock examples)
+ - **QMI8658C** IMU (for IMU examples)
+ - **AXP2101** PMU (for power management examples)
+ - **ES8311** audio codec (for audio example)
+ 
+ ## Notes
+ 
+ - Examples use &#96;embedded-graphics&#96; for drawing, which is Rust-native
+ - LVGL examples are placeholders since LVGL is C-only
+ - Audio example requires ES8311 driver implementation
+ - All examples assume proper hardware initialization (see main.rs patterns)
+ - Consider using async/await for non-blocking operations
+ - Add proper error handling in production code
+ 
+ ## Related Documentation
+ 
+ - [Device documentation](../../devices/waveshare-esp32-s3-touch-amoled-1.8.md) - Hardware reference
+ - [Display and graphics patterns](../../display-graphics.md) - Graphics programming guide
+ - [Arduino patterns reference](../../devices/waveshare-amoled-1.8-arduino-patterns.md) - Original Arduino patterns
+ 
```

```diff
  // Notes:
- // - The original example uses random text sizes, but embedded-graphics
- //   MonoTextStyle uses fixed font sizes. For variable sizes, use different fonts
- //   or scale the text using transformations
- // - Random number generation can use esp_hal::rng::Rng
- // - Consider using a framebuffer for smoother updates
+ // - The original Arduino example uses &#96;random()&#96; which generates values from 0 to RAND_MAX
+ // - In Rust, use &#96;esp_hal::rng::Rng&#96; for hardware random number generation
+ // - RGB565 color format uses 16 bits: 5 bits red, 6 bits green, 5 bits blue
+ // - Text scaling in embedded-graphics requires using different font sizes or manual scaling
+ // - The original uses &#96;setTextSize(x_scale, y_scale, pixel_margin)&#96; which embedded-graphics
+ //   doesn't directly support - you'd need to implement scaling manually or use different fonts
+ // - Consider using a framebuffer for smoother updates and to avoid full screen clears
```

```diff
  //! ## What This Example Does
  //!
- //! - Initializes the FT3168 capacitive touch controller via I2C
- //! - Sets up the display with a brightness fade-in animation
- //! - Shows "Loading board" text during initialization
- //! - In the main loop, continuously monitors for touch events
- //! - When a touch is detected, draws a blue circle (radius 5) at the touch coordinates
- //! - Only draws if touch coordinates are greater than 20 pixels from the edges (to avoid
- //!   drawing in the margin area)
- //!
- //! ## When This Could Be Useful
- //!
- //! - Testing touch controller functionality and calibration
- //! - Creating interactive drawing or note-taking applications
- //! - Demonstrating touch input handling patterns
- //! - As a foundation for touch-based UI interactions
- //! - Educational purposes to understand touch coordinate mapping
- //!
- //! ## Key Patterns Demonstrated
- //!
- //! - FT3168 touch controller initialization and interrupt handling
- //! - Reading touch coordinates from the touch controller
- //! - Drawing shapes (circles) at specific coordinates
- //! - Touch event filtering (ignoring touches too close to edges)
- //!
- //! ## Notes
- //!
- //! - The touch controller uses an interrupt pin (GPIO21) for efficient touch detection
- //! - Touch coordinates are read from the FT3168's I2C registers
- //! - The example uses a simple circle drawing approach; for smoother drawing, you might
- //!   want to draw lines between consecutive touch points
- 
- // This is a conceptual example showing the key patterns.
- // In a real implementation, you would integrate this into your main.rs with proper
- // async/await patterns, error handling, and resource management.
- 
- use embedded_graphics::{
-     pixelcolor::Rgb888,
-     prelude::*,
-     primitives::{Circle, PrimitiveStyle},
- };
- 
- // Key implementation patterns:
- 
- // 1. Initialize FT3168 touch controller
- //    - Set up I2C bus for touch controller (address 0x38)
- //    - Configure touch interrupt pin (GPIO21)
- //    - Set touch power mode to monitor mode
- //    - Wait for successful initialization
- 
- // 2. Display initialization with brightness fade
- //    - Initialize display
- //    - Fill screen with white background
- //    - Fade brightness from 0 to 255 over ~765ms (255 steps * 3ms)
- //    - Display "Loading board" text during fade
- 
- // 3. Main loop - touch drawing

- //        // Check if touch interrupt flag is set

- //            let touch_y = read_touch_y();
- //            
- //            // Log touch coordinates

- //        // Small delay to avoid excessive CPU usage

- //    }
- 
- // Touch controller constants:
- // - FT3168 I2C address: 0x38
- // - Touch interrupt pin: GPIO21 (active low)
- // - Touch reset: EXIO2 via TCA9554 expander
- 
- // Display drawing patterns:
- // - Use embedded_graphics primitives for drawing
- // - Draw directly to framebuffer, then update display

+ //! - Initializes I2C bus for TCA9554 expander and FT3168 touch controller
+ //! - Configures TCA9554 expander pins (EXIO0, EXIO1, EXIO2) as outputs
+ //! - Performs reset sequence: all LOW for 20ms, then all HIGH
+ //! - Initializes FT3168 touch controller with retry loop (2 second delays)
+ //! - Sets touch power mode to MONITOR mode
+ //! - Initializes display with brightness fade-in (0-255 over ~765ms, 3ms steps)
+ //! - Shows "Loading board" text during brightness fade
+ //! - In main loop: continuously reads touch coordinates
+ //! - When touch interrupt flag is set, draws blue circle (radius 5) at touch position
+ //! - Only draws if touch coordinates are &gt; 20 pixels from edges
+ //!
+ //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //!
+ //! - Testing touch controller functionality and calibration
+ //! - Creating interactive drawing or note-taking applications
+ //! - Demonstrating touch input handling patterns
+ //! - As a foundation for touch-based UI interactions
+ //! - Educational purposes to understand touch coordinate mapping
+ //!
+ //! ## Original Arduino Code Structure
+ //!
+ //! &#96;&#96;&#96;cpp
+ //! void setup() {
+ //!   Wire.begin(IIC_SDA, IIC_SCL);
+ //!   expander.begin(0x20);

+ //!   }
+ //!
+ //!   FT3168-&gt;IIC_Write_Device_State(TOUCH_POWER_MODE, TOUCH_POWER_MONITOR);
+ //!
+ //!   gfx-&gt;begin();
+ //!   gfx-&gt;fillScreen(RGB565_WHITE);
+ //!
+ //!   for (int i = 0; i &lt;= 255; i++) {
+ //!     gfx-&gt;setBrightness(i);

+ //!     delay(3);
+ //!   }
+ //!   delay(500);
+ //!   gfx-&gt;fillScreen(RGB565_WHITE);
+ //! }
+ //!
+ //! void loop() {
+ //!   int32_t touchX = FT3168-&gt;IIC_Read_Device_Value(TOUCH_COORDINATE_X);
+ //!   int32_t touchY = FT3168-&gt;IIC_Read_Device_Value(TOUCH_COORDINATE_Y);
+ //!
```

```diff
- //! ## When This Could Be Useful
```

```diff
+ //! - Sets WiFi to station mode and disconnects from any existing connection
+ //! - Calculates display layout: banner height, graph area, channel widths
+ //! - Draws banner with "ESP32 WiFi Analyzer" text in colored segments
+ //! - Scans for WiFi networks (non-async, showing hidden networks)
+ //! - Processes each network:
+ //!   - Tracks peak RSSI per channel
+ //!   - Counts APs per channel (avoiding duplicates by BSSID prefix)
+ //!   - Calculates noise contribution across overlapping channels (±4 channels)
+ //! - Draws signal bars as ellipses for each network
+ //! - Shows SSID, RSSI, and encryption status for strong signals (RSSI &gt;= -70 dBm)
+ //! - Calculates and displays least noisy channels (channels 1-11)
+ //! - Draws channel numbers and AP counts at bottom
+ //! - Updates every 3 seconds
+ //!
+ //! ## Original Arduino Code Key Algorithms
+ //!
+ //! ### Noise Calculation
+ //! &#96;&#96;&#96;cpp
+ //! int32_t noise = rssi - RSSI_FLOOR;  // e.g., -80 - (-100) = 20
+ //! noise *= noise;  // 20 * 20 = 400
+ //! // Add to current channel and ±4 neighboring channels
+ //! if (channel &gt; 4) noise_list[idx - 4] += noise;
```

```diff
  //! ## What This Example Does
  //!
- //! - Draws a circular clock face with 60 minute marks (12 hour marks are larger)
- //! - Displays three hands: hour (white), minute (blue), and second (red)
- //! - Updates the clock every second with smooth hand movement
- //! - Uses cached drawing to efficiently erase old hand positions
- //! - Starts from the compile time (from &#96;__TIME__&#96; macro in C, or system time in Rust)
- //! - Handles hand overlap correctly (minute hand doesn't overwrite second hand, etc.)
- //!
- //! ## When This Could Be Useful
- //!
- //! - Creating clock applications or watch faces
- //! - Demonstrating smooth animation techniques
- //! - Testing graphics performance with frequent updates
- //! - Educational purposes to understand trigonometry and coordinate calculations
- //! - As a foundation for more complex clock applications (alarms, timers, etc.)
- //!
- //! ## Key Patterns Demonstrated
- //!
- //! - Trigonometric calculations for hand positions (sin/cos)
- //! - Efficient screen updates using cached pixel positions
- //! - Hand overlap detection and drawing order
- //! - Smooth animation with millisecond precision
- //! - Circular mark drawing for clock face
- //!
- //! ## Clock Face Design
- //!
- //! - Background: Black
- //! - Hour marks: White, longer marks every 15 minutes (12, 3, 6, 9 o'clock)
- //! - 5-minute marks: White, medium length
- //! - Minute marks: Dark grey, shorter
- //! - Hour hand: White, 3/8 of radius length
- //! - Minute hand: Blue, 2/3 of radius length
```

```diff
  //! ## What This Example Does
  //!
- //! - Initializes the ES8311 audio codec via I2C
- //! - Configures I2S interface for audio input/output
- //! - Sets up microphone gain and voice volume
- //! - Plays a test sound (canon PCM data) on startup
- //! - Continuously reads audio from microphone and plays it back through speaker
- //! - Creates a real-time audio loopback/echo effect
+ //! - Initializes serial communication at 115200 baud with debug output
+ //! - Enables amplifier (PA pin = GPIO46, set HIGH)
+ //! - Configures I2S interface:
+ //!   - Mode: I2S_MODE_STD (standard I2S)
+ //!   - Sample rate: 16000 Hz
+ //!   - Bit width: 16-bit
+ //!   - Slot mode: STEREO
+ //!   - Slot: BOTH (input and output)
+ //! - Initializes ES8311 codec via I2C:
+ //!   - MCLK frequency: sample_rate * 256 = 4,096,000 Hz
+ //!   - MCLK from MCLK pin (not internal)
+ //!   - Resolution: 16-bit for both ADC and DAC
+ //!   - Microphone: differential mode (false)
+ //!   - Voice volume: 85% (0-100 scale)
+ //!   - Microphone gain: Level 3 (0-7 scale)
+ //! - Plays test sound (canon PCM data) on startup
+ //! - Continuously reads audio from microphone and plays it back (echo/loopback)
+ //! - Uses 10KB receive buffer for audio data
  //!
- //! ## When This Could Be Useful
+ //! ## Original Arduino Code
  //!
- //! - Testing audio hardware (microphone and speaker)
- //! - Verifying I2S communication with ES8311 codec
- //! - Creating voice recording applications
- //! - Building audio processing applications
- //! - Demonstrating audio I/O capabilities
- //! - Testing audio latency and quality
- //!
- //! ## Key Patterns Demonstrated
- //!
- //! - ES8311 codec initialization and configuration
- //! - I2S interface setup for audio streaming
- //! - Audio buffer management
- //! - Real-time audio processing loop
- //! - Microphone gain and volume control
- //!
- //! ## Audio Configuration
- //!
```
